A collaborator shares a dataset with hundreds of millions of rows,
already written to disk in an efficient columnar format -- a multi-season
multi-environment trial, a genomic panel, a sensor archive. You want to
fit a Bayesian mixed model, but the data will not fit in memory, and
pushing every row through a sampler would be hopeless. This vignette
shows how `flexybayes_stream()` fits such a model exactly, with memory
that does not grow with the row count.

**The envelope, stated once.** What the method delivers is exact
cell-likelihood aggregation for iid exponential-family models with a
small cell count, read from partitioned `.fst`, and fitted on INLA.
Every one of those conditions is load-bearing: outside them the package
refuses by name rather than approximating. The section *When aggregation
does not apply* says which structures fall outside and why.

Every chunk on this page runs, against real `.fst` files written to a
temporary directory and small enough to fit in seconds. The two
benchmark tables further down are a different kind of evidence: they are
recorded from an external run on data that does not fit that
description, tens of gigabytes on disk, and the code that produced them
is shown but not executed here.

# 1. The idea: aggregate exactly, then fit

The data is almost always massively replicated -- the same handful of
environments crossed with the same genotypes, over and over. For the
exponential-family models flexyBayes targets, the likelihood of a *cell*
(a set of rows that share the same linear predictor) depends on the rows
only through a few *sufficient statistics*, and those statistics are
additive across any partition of the rows. They can therefore be
accumulated one chunk at a time and the chunks discarded.

For a cell $k$ with $n_k$ rows sharing the linear predictor $\eta_k$:

- gaussian (identity link) needs $\sum y_i$ and $\sum y_i^2$. The cell
  log-likelihood is algebraically identical to the per-row form, so this
  is exact, not approximate.
- poisson (log link) needs $\sum y_i$ and $\sum E_i$ (exposure), because
  independent Poissons with a shared rate add.
- binomial (logit link) needs $\sum y_i$ (successes) and $\sum m_i$
  (trials), because independent Binomials with a shared probability add.

In every case the cell statistics are sums, and a sum over the whole
dataset is the sum of the sums over its chunks. The fitted posterior is
the full-data posterior. The cost of the fit is set by the number of
distinct cells $K$, not the number of rows $N$.

# 2. Fitting from an `.fst` file

The realistic delivery format is a columnar file on disk.
`flexybayes_stream()` reads it in row-range chunks, accumulates the
sufficient statistics, and fits the $K$-cell model through INLA --
the only active fitting engine for the aggregated path (naming a
withdrawn or otherwise unrecognised backend refuses with a structured
`unknown_backend` message -- see `NEWS.md`, 0.9.3). Peak memory is one
chunk plus the small cell accumulator, never the full table.


``` r
library(flexyBayes)
library(fst)
set.seed(20260815L)
```

The trial below is the same design the in-memory identity check further
down reuses: six environments, forty genotypes, three replicates.


``` r
n_env <- 6L
n_gen <- 40L
n_rep <- 3L

trial_df <- expand.grid(
  rep = seq_len(n_rep),
  genotype = factor(seq_len(n_gen)),
  environment = factor(paste0("E", seq_len(n_env)))
)
g_eff <- rnorm(n_gen, sd = 0.7)
trial_df$yield <- 5 +
  as.numeric(trial_df$environment) * 0.4 +
  g_eff[as.integer(trial_df$genotype)] +
  rnorm(nrow(trial_df), sd = 0.5)

nrow(trial_df)                                             # rows
#> [1] 720
nlevels(trial_df$environment) * nlevels(trial_df$genotype) # cells K
#> [1] 240
```

Seven hundred and twenty rows across 240 design cells, a compression of
three -- nothing at this size, and that is the point: the streamed route
below has to agree with the in-memory one where both are cheap, before
the claim is worth anything at a scale where only one is possible.
Written to disk and streamed back:


``` r
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".fst")
fst::write_fst(trial_df, path)

fit <- flexybayes_stream(
  yield ~ environment,         # fixed factor(s)
  random  = ~ genotype,        # random-intercept grouping factor
  source  = path,               # an .fst path on disk
  family  = "gaussian",
  backend = "inla",
  chunk_rows = 5e6              # rows read per chunk
)
#> chunk 1/1: 720 rows read, K = 240 cells
#> fitting 240 cells (compression 3:1) on backend 'inla'
fit
#> Bayesian mixed model  [flexyBayes / aggregated-gaussian]
#> ------------------------------------------------------------ 
#>   family:     gaussian ( identity link)
#>   N obs:      720 
#>   K cells:    240 
#>   fixed:      2 
#>   random:     1 
#>   backend:    (path = )
#>   runtime:    2.23 sec
#>   Representation: exact (model, not inference)
#>   Engine:         (unknown engine)
#>   aggregation: N = 720 rows -> K = 240 cells (ratio 3:1)
#>   priors:     per-row-equivalent (default prior; aggregated posterior matches per-row) 
#> ------------------------------------------------------------ 
#>   $glm      -- per-row reconstructed fitted values + coef shim
#>   $inla     -- raw aggregated INLA fit (use INLA's summary etc.)
#>   $extras   -- summary, aggregation_meta, backend_decision
summary(fit)
#> Bayesian mixed model summary  [flexyBayes / aggregated-gaussian]
#> ============================================================== 
#>   Fixed    : yield ~ environment 
#>   Random   : ~genotype 
#>   Model    : G: genotype iid; R: units 
#>   aggregation: N = 720 rows -> K = 240 cells (ratio 3:1)
#>   Family   : gaussian / identity 
#>   Engine   : INLA nested Laplace approximation 
#>   N        : 720 design rows, 720 observed responses
#>   Runtime  : 2.2 sec
#> 
#> -- Fixed effects (posterior mean, 95% credible interval) --------
#>           term estimate std.error conf.low conf.high
#>    (Intercept)   5.2760    0.1263   5.0275    5.5245
#>  environmentE2   0.4167    0.0662   0.2868    0.5467
#>  environmentE3   0.7471    0.0662   0.6172    0.8771
#>  environmentE4   1.1573    0.0662   1.0273    1.2872
#>  environmentE5   1.5029    0.0662   1.3730    1.6328
#>  environmentE6   1.9430    0.0662   1.8130    2.0729
#> 
#> -- Variance components (95% credible interval) ------------------
#> Estimate = posterior mean (not REML). Prior column is the prior that was used.
#>    component estimate std.error conf.low conf.high          prior note
#>        sigma   0.5130    0.0139   0.4864    0.5410 engine default     
#>  sd_genotype   0.7395    0.0846   0.5907    0.9223 engine default     
#> 
#> -- Convergence -----------------------------------------------
#>   Engine    : INLA nested Laplace approximation
#>   Mode status: 0 (0 = converged)
#>   Marginal log-likelihood: -157.524
#>   Largest symmetric KLD between the Gaussian approximation and the
#>   corrected marginal: 1.93e-08
```

For a dataset shared as several partitioned shards -- the usual shape for
genuinely large data -- pass the vector of shard paths and they are
streamed in turn with the same bounded footprint.


``` r
shard_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "trial_shards")
dir.create(shard_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

shard_idx <- cut(seq_len(nrow(trial_df)), breaks = 3L, labels = FALSE)
shards <- vapply(seq_len(3L), function(s) {
  p <- file.path(shard_dir, sprintf("shard_%d.fst", s))
  fst::write_fst(trial_df[shard_idx == s, ], p)
  p
}, character(1L))

fit_shards <- flexybayes_stream(
  yield ~ environment, random = ~ genotype,
  source = shards, family = "gaussian", backend = "inla",
  verbose = FALSE
)
summary(fit_shards)
#> Bayesian mixed model summary  [flexyBayes / aggregated-gaussian]
#> ============================================================== 
#>   Fixed    : yield ~ environment 
#>   Random   : ~genotype
```

To inspect the compression a design will achieve before committing to a
fit, pass `fit = FALSE` and the function returns the aggregation summary.


``` r
agg <- flexybayes_stream(
  yield ~ environment, random = ~ genotype,
  source = path, fit = FALSE
)
#> chunk 1/1: 720 rows read, K = 240 cells
agg          # prints N, K, and the compression ratio
#> <fb_aggregated>: N = 720 rows -> K = 240 cells (compression 3.0:1)
#>   fixed cols:  (Intercept), environmentE2, environmentE3, environmentE4, environmentE5, environmentE6
#>   random grps: genotype
#>   response:    yield
```

Binomial and poisson models fit the same way. A bare 0/1 response is
treated as Bernoulli, one trial per row -- where the data instead carries a
trial count per row, name that column with `trials =`. For poisson, name
an exposure column with `exposure =` if the data carries one.


``` r
n_plot <- 200L
germ_df <- data.frame(
  treatment = factor(sample(paste0("T", 1:4), n_plot, replace = TRUE)),
  block     = factor(sample(paste0("B", 1:8), n_plot, replace = TRUE)),
  m         = sample(20:30, n_plot, replace = TRUE)
)
p_trt <- c(T1 = 0.5, T2 = 0.6, T3 = 0.7, T4 = 0.8)
germ_df$germinated <- rbinom(n_plot, germ_df$m, p_trt[as.character(germ_df$treatment)])

germ_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".fst")
fst::write_fst(germ_df, germ_path)

fit_bin <- flexybayes_stream(
  germinated ~ treatment, random = ~ block,
  source = germ_path, family = "binomial", trials = "m",
  backend = "inla", verbose = FALSE
)
summary(fit_bin)
#> Bayesian mixed model summary  [flexyBayes / aggregated-binomial]
#> ============================================================== 
#>   Fixed    : germinated ~ treatment 
#>   Random   : ~block 
#>   Model    : G: block iid; R: units 
#>   aggregation: N = 200 rows -> K = 32 cells (ratio 6:1)
#>   Family   : binomial / logit 
#>   Engine   : INLA nested Laplace approximation

#>   Runtime  : 2 sec

#> 
#> -- Variance components (95% credible interval) ------------------
#> Estimate = posterior mean (not REML). Prior column is the prior that was used.
#>  component estimate std.error conf.low conf.high          prior note
```

``` r
n_obs <- 200L
count_df <- data.frame(
  treatment = factor(sample(paste0("T", 1:3), n_obs, replace = TRUE)),
  site      = factor(sample(paste0("S", 1:8), n_obs, replace = TRUE)),
  area      = runif(n_obs, 0.5, 2)
)
mu_trt <- c(T1 = 3, T2 = 5, T3 = 7)
count_df$count <- rpois(n_obs, mu_trt[as.character(count_df$treatment)] * count_df$area)

count_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".fst")
fst::write_fst(count_df, count_path)

fit_pois <- flexybayes_stream(
  count ~ treatment, random = ~ site,
  source = count_path, family = "poisson", exposure = "area",
  backend = "inla", verbose = FALSE
)
summary(fit_pois)
```

# 3. The aggregation identity, checked in memory

The exactness claim is also checkable on data that fits in memory, and
this section checks it, reusing the trial simulated above. When the data
does fit, the ordinary entry `flexybayes()` reaches the same aggregation
through `aggregate = "auto"` (the default) on `backend = "inla"`, for the
gaussian, binomial, and poisson families. Fitting the same data both ways
should return the same posterior, not a similar one.


``` r
fit_agg <- flexybayes(
  yield ~ environment, random = ~ genotype,
  data = trial_df, backend = "inla", verbose = FALSE
)                                            # auto-aggregates

fit_row <- flexybayes(
  yield ~ environment, random = ~ genotype,
  data = trial_df, backend = "inla", aggregate = FALSE,
  verbose = FALSE
)                                            # per row
```


``` r
round(cbind(
  aggregated = coef(fit_agg),
  per_row = coef(fit_row),
  difference = coef(fit_agg) - coef(fit_row)
), 6)
#>               aggregated  per_row difference
#> (Intercept)     5.275970 5.275971          0
#> environmentE2   0.416732 0.416732          0
#> environmentE3   0.747117 0.747117          0
#> environmentE4   1.157252 1.157252          0
#> environmentE5   1.502889 1.502888          0
#> environmentE6   1.942981 1.942981          0
```

The fixed-effect posterior means agree. That is the aggregation identity
rather than a tolerance being met: the aggregated likelihood is the
per-row likelihood rewritten, so the same approximation applied to both
returns the same answer. Scaling the row count changes how long the
accumulation takes and nothing about the model.

# 4. What it costs: per-row versus aggregated

**External benchmark.** The two tables in this section and the next were
measured outside the package on a 32 GB machine. They are not produced
when this vignette is built and nothing here re-runs them. The full
measurement record -- what was run, on what hardware, and where the
claim stops -- is *inst/validation/benchmark_scaling.md*, shipped with
the package -- these two tables are excerpted from it.

The first table compares the two paths at sample sizes where both are
feasible, on a 6-environment by 60-genotype design (360 cells) with a
gaussian random intercept and the INLA backend. Memory is the operating
system peak resident size of a fresh process.

| method   |        N | wall (s) | peak (MB) | intercept |
|----------|---------:|---------:|----------:|----------:|
| per row  |  100,000 |     5.2  |     1,346 |   1.36265 |
| per row  |  500,000 |    15.3  |     6,386 |   1.35696 |
| per row  | 1,000,000|    19.0  |    12,352 |   1.34918 |
| per row  | 5,000,000| infeasible -- exceeded the memory budget | | |
| streamed |  100,000 |     2.9  |       399 |   1.36265 |
| streamed | 1,000,000|     2.8  |       470 |   1.34918 |
| streamed |50,000,000|     4.0  |     3,712 |   1.35482 |

The per-row path's time and memory grow with $N$ -- 12 GB at one million
rows -- and it became infeasible at five million on a 32 GB machine. The
streamed path returns the same intercept (1.34918 against 1.34918 at one
million rows) in about three seconds.

# 5. How far it scales

**External benchmark, as above.** The next table streams a partitioned
`.fst` dataset on a 6-environment by 200-genotype design (1200 cells).
The dataset is written as 50-million-row shards and streamed in
five-million-row chunks. Note the shape of the source: partitioned
`.fst` is the configuration these numbers describe, and it is the one
the envelope names. A single file past `2^31 - 1` rows refuses rather
than streaming, because its row count cannot be recorded as an integer.

| N             |    K | wall (s) | peak (MB) | on disk (GB) | intercept |
|---------------|-----:|---------:|----------:|-------------:|----------:|
| 10,000,000    | 1200 |    3.3   |       708 |        0.09  |   0.98542 |
| 100,000,000   | 1200 |    5.7   |       796 |        0.94  |   0.98552 |
| 1,000,000,000 | 1200 |   31.9   |       844 |        9.40  |   0.98565 |
| 5,000,000,000 | 1200 |  150.9   |       846 |       46.98  |   0.98568 |

Peak memory is essentially flat -- 708 MB at ten million rows, 846 MB at
five billion -- because only one chunk plus the 1200-cell accumulator is
ever resident. A five-billion-row gaussian mixed model fits exactly in
about two and a half minutes of streaming, reading 47 GB of shards once
from disk. The recovered intercept is stable across all four scales: the
data volume grows five-hundred-fold while the memory footprint and the
fitted estimate do not move.

# 6. When aggregation does not apply

The method compresses only when the design is low-cardinality. A
continuous fixed covariate gives one cell per distinct value, so there is
no compression, and the model is refused before any data is read. Random
slopes, structured covariance, and smooth terms make the linear predictor
vary within a cell, which breaks the cell-constant property, and they are
refused with a named reason code rather than silently approximated. A
non-Bernoulli binomial response needs per-row trial counts that the cell
sums cannot recover, so it too falls back to the per-row path. The
guiding principle is that flexyBayes scales by preserving the model's
meaning, and refuses loudly where exact aggregation does not hold, rather
than hiding an approximation behind the same interface. For any of these
models, fit the data per row with `flexybayes()`.

# 7. How the Gaussian case stays exact

The identity checked above is not a coincidence of this design -- the
mechanism is stated in the header of `R/emit_gaussian_aggregated.R`. On
the INLA path, cell means enter the fit as a weighted gaussian
likelihood, weight $n_k$ per cell -- so far, an ordinary
inverse-variance-weighted regression on the cell means. What that
likelihood alone would drop is the within-cell sum of squares, which
depends on $\sigma$ and cannot be recovered from a cell mean -- the header
folds it into the prior on the log-precision instead, as a custom
`expression:` prior with $a = \mathrm{WSS}/2$ and $b = (N - K)/2$, so
that cell-level and row-level posteriors on $\beta$ and $\sigma$
coincide. The source states the expression itself:

> `prior_expr <- "expression: a = (WSS / 2) + 5e-5; b = (N - K) / 2 + 1;`
> `log_dens = -a * exp(theta) + b * theta; return(log_dens);"`

and explains what the two constants do: "The constants `a` and `b`
collapse the default `loggamma(1, 5e-5)` precision prior with the
`Delta(theta)` correction. The combined prior is fed via
`control.family$hyper$prec$prior` and INLA's deterministic numerical
engine recovers the per-row posterior on beta + sigma to bit-exact
precision (spike: differences <= 1e-4 on a 1000-row example)." The
`5e-5` and `+ 1` terms visible in the quoted expression are that same
default precision prior's own regularising constants, folded into the
closed form rather than added on top of it -- the idealised $a =
\mathrm{WSS}/2$, $b = (N-K)/2$ is what they reduce to as those constants
vanish. `micro-compare` above is this equivalence, run rather than taken
on the header's word.
